name: Praxis
comment: Fallback highlighting for .px files: it works before the language server attaches, while it is restarting, and in any non-LSP renderer. It emits the SAME TextMate scopes the server's semantic tokens are mapped onto in package.json's semanticTokenScopes, so a file does not change colour when the server connects. Four Rust tests in crates/praxis-cli/tests/grammar.rs read this file and check its keyword, atomic and constructor patterns against the compiler's own closed tables — a grammar's word lists are copies that no compiler checks, and the failure (a word quietly stops being coloured) is one nobody files.

block-comment.comment: Nestable: /* /* */ */ is ONE comment (SyntaxKind::BlockComment). A flat rule closes at the first */ and paints the rest of the file as code.
block-comment.name: comment.block.praxis

keywords.comment: Every keyword in SyntaxKind's table. Checked against SyntaxKind::all_keyword_texts() by a Rust test, because this list is a copy the compiler does not see.
keywords.name: keyword.control.praxis

update-operator.comment: `min=` / `max=` are contextual operators built from an identifier plus `=` (UPDATE_OP), not keywords — the lexer cannot claim `min` without taking it from every program that names the prelude helper. The lookahead is what keeps a plain `min(a, b)` an ordinary call.

strings.comment: A text literal may not span a line (the lexer refuses one, T004), so the rule ends at the line even when the quote is unclosed.
strings.name: string.quoted.double.praxis

numbers.comment: §4.12 allows `.5` and `2.`, and `..`/`..=` is a range and never part of a float. The negative lookahead after a trailing dot, and the negative lookbehind before a leading one, are what keep `1..2` from painting as two floats.

types.comment: A capitalized identifier is a type name: §4.1's convention, and the only thing a regex can tell. The semantic layer knows the difference between `Grid[T]` and a local called `Grid`; this is the approximation it refines.
types.name: entity.name.type.praxis

read-region.comment: §7.1 enters the parser-expression sublanguage at `read` (and at `parse`'s second argument, which a regex grammar cannot find without counting commas — inside a `parse` call the semantic layer supplies the parser classes on its own). The region ends at the end of the line or at a delimiter it did not open; a constructor's own parenthesis opens a sub-rule, so a parser expression broken across lines stays inside it. Constructors are contextual (`lines` is an ordinary identifier outside a parser expression) and this is the approximation §6.3 allows: the semantic layer corrects it, and the disagreement resolves toward the compiler.

parser-call.comment: Every §7.5 constructor. Checked against Constructor::ALL by a Rust test.

parser-named-argument.comment: `rules: lines(int)`, `skip: whitespace`, `fill: 0` — §7.5's named arguments. Which names are *keyword* arguments is the constructor's question and not a regex's; both get the same scope, and the semantic layer distinguishes them.

parser-flags.comment: `ragged` is §7.5's one bare-keyword argument; the other three are `skip:`'s policy values (SkipPolicy::ALL).
parser-flags.name: variable.parameter.parser.praxis

capture-type.comment: Every §7.4 atomic. Checked against AtomicKind::ALL by a Rust test.
capture-type.name: support.type.capture.praxis

parser-template.comment: ADR-094: a template ends at the line it opens on. The `(?=\n)` alternative is what keeps an unterminated backtick from painting the rest of the file as a string — the lexer draws the same bound, with two distinct token kinds so the state is unrepresentable rather than re-derived.
parser-template.name: string.quoted.other.template.praxis

template-escape.comment: §7.2's whitespace policies and the two character escapes.
template-escape.name: constant.character.escape.praxis

template-capture.comment: `{name:type}`, `{type}` and `{name:constructor(...)}` scope their parts separately — which is what makes §19.11 criterion 4 visible before the server attaches.

patterns.comment: The capture NAME, anchored at the capture's start so only a leading `ident :` is one. `{int}` has no name and falls through to the capture-type rule; `{c:one_of(":")}`'s inner colon is inside a nested rule and never reaches here.
